title: Weekly Reading Rundown - What People Have Been Writing This Week
author: Sarah Findlater
summary: Sarah Findlater's weekly curated digest rounds up six education Substack posts she found notable that week, each accompanied by a short editorial gloss explaining its argument and why it earned a place on the list. The selections span curriculum design (Carl Hendrick on why retrieval and spacing require deliberate curriculum architecture, not just visible routines like starter quizzes), instructional leadership (Haili Hughes on how school priorities distort as they cascade to classrooms), and epistemic humility about cognitive science itself (Dylan Kane weighing what the science of learning does and does not explain about classroom complexity). It also includes Natalie Wexler's argument for teaching social studies as knowledge-building for literacy without reducing it to a mere literacy vehicle, and Dan Meyer's methodologically careful comparison of Alpha School's AI-led model across selective and non-selective settings to separate the effect of the pedagogy from the effect of pupil selection. Findlater closes the roundup with a lighter entry, Andrew Marsh's Star-Wars-themed account of a failed school-lunch improvement saga, and an open invitation for readers to submit posts for future rundowns. As a curated digest with substantive editorial framing on each item rather than a bare link list, the roundup has independent archival value beyond its individual linked articles.
points: Curates six education Substack posts spanning curriculum design, instructional leadership, and epistemic humility about cognitive science, each with the curator's own explanatory gloss rather than a bare link.
Highlights Dan Meyer's methodologically careful comparison of Alpha School's AI-led model across selective and non-selective settings, isolating the model's effect from the effect of pupil selection.
Includes Dylan Kane's argument that cognitive science, while valuable, remains incomplete against the full complexity of classroom practice and teachers' tacit professional knowledge.
Balances serious curriculum and leadership pieces with a lighter, narrative entry (Andrew Marsh's school-lunch saga), reflecting the roundup's mixed inspirational and analytical purpose.
quotes: Carl Hendrick argues that retrieval and spacing depend on curriculum design, with deliberate routes back to earlier knowledge.
Dr Haili Hughes writes, very funnily, about how a carefully explained school priority can become something quite different by the time it reaches classrooms.

Dylan Kane considers both the contribution and the limits of the science of learning. He argues that cognitive science has much to offer teachers, but remains incomplete when faced with the complexity of classrooms.
Natalie Wexler examines how teaching history and social studies can strengthen reading comprehension by building pupils' knowledge and vocabulary.
Dan Meyer looks closely at Alpha School's claims that pupils can learn far more quickly through an AI-led, two-hour model.
Andrew Marsh tells the very funny story of trying to improve school lunches in a small rural school.
